claim: A system is intuitive to use when a user can interact effectively, not-consciously using previous knowledge.
evidence: p. 129: “A technical system is, in the context of a certain task, intuitively usable while the particular user is able to interact effectively, not-consciously using previous knowledge.” (definition version 1.1)

claim: Prior knowledge lies on a continuum: innate, sensorimotor, culture, expertise.
evidence: pp. 130–132, Fig. 1 “Continuum of knowledge in intuitive interaction”; p. 131: “The first and lowest level of the continuum consists of innate knowledge” … “The most specific level of knowledge is expertise”.

claim: Both research groups define intuitive interaction as the non-conscious use of prior knowledge and propose a continuum of prior knowledge.
evidence: Abstract: definitions involve “the non-conscious use of prior knowledge”; the authors devised “a continuum of prior knowledge”. Levels not shown in the abstract.

claim: Image schemas and their metaphorical extensions can serve as patterns for intuitive interaction.
evidence: Title only. Read the paper before citing for anything beyond its title.

claim: [Ours] Criterion 3 excludes only the expertise end of the continuum.
evidence: Our application of the continuum to the inclusion rule.

claim: [Ours] Mappings grounded in crossmodal correspondences draw on knowledge at the innate or sensorimotor end.
evidence: Our inference. Partial support: Stiles & Shimojo (2015) attribute naive performance to crossmodal correspondences, but do not use the continuum.

claim: Naive participants, not told the encoding and given no feedback, matched sensory-substitution sounds to images above chance; the authors call this intuitive.
evidence: “Entirely naive participants were found to match vOICe sounds to images significantly above chance (Expt. 1).” “Naive participants were not told the vOICe encoding scheme…” “Feedback on performance was not provided.”

claim: The authors attribute this intuitive performance to crossmodal correspondences.
evidence: “crossmodal correspondences underlie vOICe intuitiveness” (Expt. 2 discussion).

claim: Caveat: the task was forced-choice matching of static images, and the authors say training is still needed for real use.
evidence: Their limitations section; blind groups had four participants each.
